claim: Children undergoing cancer treatments are at risk for impaired fertility.
source: Children undergoing cancer treatments are at risk for impaired fertility.
evidence: Supported by citations to Allen et al., 2018 and Miller et al., 2016 in the abstract.

claim: Cryopreserved prepubertal testicular biopsies could theoretically be later matured in vitro to produce spermatozoa for assisted reproductive technology.
source: Cryopreserved prepubertal testicular biopsies could theoretically be later matured in vitro to produce spermatozoa for assisted reproductive technology.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications.

claim: A complete in vitro spermatogenesis has been obtained from mouse prepubertal testicular tissue, although with low efficiency.
source: A complete in vitro spermatogenesis has been obtained from mouse prepubertal testicular tissue, although with low efficiency.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Steroid hormones are essential for the progression of spermatogenesis.
source: Steroid hormones are essential for the progression of spermatogenesis, the aim of this study was to investigate steroidogenesis and steroid signaling in organotypic cultures.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Transcript levels of adult Leydig cells and steroidogenic markers were decreased after 30 days of culture.
source: Despite a conserved density of Leydig cells after 30 days of culture (D30), transcript levels of adult Leydig cells and steroidogenic markers were decreased.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Increased amounts of progesterone and estradiol and reduced androstenedione levels were observed at D30.
source: Increased amounts of progesterone and estradiol and reduced androstenedione levels were observed at D30, together with decreased transcript levels of steroid metabolizing genes and steroid target genes.
evidence: This is supported by steroid hormone measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: hCG was insufficient to facilitate Leydig cell differentiation, restore steroidogenesis, and improve sperm yield.
source: hCG was insufficient to facilitate Leydig cell differentiation, restore steroidogenesis, and improve sperm yield.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from hCG supplementation experiments.

claim: This study reports the failure of adult Leydig cell development and altered steroid production and signaling in tissue cultures.
source: In conclusion, this study reports the failure of adult Leydig cell development and altered steroid production and signaling in tissue cultures.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in the study.

claim: The organotypic culture system will need to be further improved before it can be translated into clinics for childhood cancer survivors.
source: The organotypic culture system will need to be further improved before it can be translated into clinics for childhood cancer survivors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of impaired steroidogenesis and low efficiency.

claim: Pediatric cancer treatments such as chemotherapy have recognized toxicity in germline stem cells, which could lead to infertility in adulthood.
source: Pediatric cancer treatments such as chemotherapy have recognized toxicity in germline stem cells, which could lead to infertility in adulthood (Allen et al., 2018; Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Allen et al., 2018 and Miller et al., 2016.

claim: Freezing of prepubertal testicular tissue containing spermatogonia is a fertility preservation option proposed for prepubertal boys with cancer prior to highly gonadotoxic treatments.
source: Freezing of prepubertal testicular tissue containing spermatogonia is a fertility preservation option proposed for prepubertal boys with cancer prior to highly gonadotoxic treatments.
evidence: This is established clinical practice based on scientific knowledge.

claim: In vitro maturation strategies are currently being optimized in animal models.
source: In vitro maturation strategies are currently being optimized in animal models.
evidence: This is a statement about current research practices.

claim: In vitro spermatogenesis could be proposed to patients with testicular localization of residual tumor cells, for whom testicular tissue autografting is not indicated (about 30% of patients with acute leukemia).
source: In vitro spermatogenesis could indeed be proposed to patients with testicular localization of residual tumor cells, for whom testicular tissue autografting is not indicated (about 30% of patients with acute leukemia).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential clinical applications with a cited statistic.

claim: The organotypic culture procedure has been used successfully to obtain spermatozoa from fresh or frozen/thawed mouse prepubertal testicular tissues.
source: The organotypic culture procedure, which preserves testicular tissue architecture, microenvironment, and cell interactions, has been used successfully to obtain spermatozoa from fresh or frozen/thawed mouse prepubertal testicular tissues (Sato et al., 2011; Yokonishi et al., 2014; Arkoun et al., 2015; Dumont et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Viable and fertile mouse offspring have been obtained from in vitro produced spermatozoa by oocyte microinjection.
source: In addition, viable and fertile mouse offspring have been obtained from in vitro produced spermatozoa by oocyte microinjection (Sato et al., 2011; Yokonishi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sato et al., 2011 and Yokonishi et al., 2014.

claim: Supplementing organotypic culture media with retinol improves the in vitro production of spermatids and spermatozoa in prepubertal mouse testicular tissues cultured at a gas-liquid interphase.
source: It has been previously shown that supplementing organotypic culture media with retinol improves the in vitro production of spermatids and spermatozoa in prepubertal mouse testicular tissues cultured at a gas-liquid interphase (Arkoun et al., 2015; Dumont et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arkoun et al., 2015 and Dumont et al., 2016.

claim: In vitro sperm production remains a rare event.
source: However, in vitro sperm production still remains a rare event.
evidence: This is an observation based on previous research findings.

claim: Transcript levels of the androgen receptor (AR)-regulated gene Rhox5 were decreased at the end of the culture period.
source: Transcript levels of the androgen receptor (AR)-regulated gene Rhox5 were decreased at the end of the culture period, suggesting that testosterone production by Leydig cells and/or AR transcriptional activity was impaired in organotypic cultures (Rondanino et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rondanino et al., 2017.

claim: A decline in intratesticular testosterone levels has been highlighted in vitro in 35- to 49 day cultures of 5 dpp mouse testes.
source: A decline in intratesticular testosterone levels has been highlighted in vitro in 35- to 49 day cultures of 5 dpp mouse testes, i.e., after the end of the first wave of spermatogenesis (Pence et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pence et al., 2019.

claim: Recent transcriptomic analysis reveals a decline in mRNA levels of Cyp17a1 in 4- to 30 day cultures of 6 dpp mouse testes.
source: Moreover, our recent transcriptomic analysis reveals a decline in mRNA levels of Cyp17a1, encoding a steroidogenic enzyme, in 4- to 30 day cultures of 6 dpp mouse testes (Dumont et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dumont et al., 2023.

claim: Two distinct populations of Leydig cells appear during mouse testicular development: fetal Leydig cells and adult Leydig cells.
source: Two distinct populations of Leydig cells appear during mouse testicular development: (i) fetal Leydig cells arising during embryonic development and regressing over the first two weeks of postnatal life and (ii) adult Leydig cells appearing around one week after birth.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mouse testicular development.

claim: 17β-HSD3 is expressed only by adult Leydig cells.
source: Although they both express StAR (steroidogenic acute regulatory protein), CYP11A1 (P450 side chain cleavage), 3β-HSD1 (3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1), and CYP17A1 (P450 17α-hydroxylase/C17-20 lyase), which are steroidogenic proteins required for androgen production, 17β-HSD3 (17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 3), which converts androstenedione to testosterone, is expressed only by adult Leydig cells (O'Shaughnessy et al., 2002; Sararols et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to O'Shaughnessy et al., 2002 and Sararols et al., 2021.

claim: The major androgens produced in fetal Leydig cells and adult Leydig cells are androstenedione and testosterone, respectively.
source: Consequently, the major androgens produced in fetal Leydig cells and adult Leydig cells are androstenedione and testosterone, respectively (O'Shaughnessy et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to O'Shaughnessy et al., 2000.

claim: In rodents, adult Leydig cells develop from undifferentiated stem Leydig cells through two intermediate cells, progenitor Leydig cells and immature Leydig cells.
source: In rodents, adult Leydig cells develop from undifferentiated stem Leydig cells through two intermediate cells, progenitor Leydig cells and immature Leydig cells (Ye et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ye et al., 2017.

claim: All Leydig cell lineage cells except stem Leydig cells express CYP11A1, 3β-HSD1, and CYP17A1.
source: All these cells, except stem Leydig cells, express CYP11A1, 3β-HSD1, and CYP17A1 (Jiang et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jiang et al., 2014 and Zhang et al., 2004.

claim: 17β-HSD3 begins to be expressed in immature Leydig cells.
source: 17β-HSD3 begins to be expressed in immature Leydig cells (Ge and Hardy, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ge and Hardy, 1998.

claim: The expression of SRD5A1, which is high in progenitor and immature Leydig cells, is silenced in adult Leydig cells.
source: The expression of the androgen metabolizing enzyme SRD5A1 (5α-reductase 1), which is high in progenitor and immature Leydig cells, is silenced in adult Leydig cells (Ge and Hardy, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ge and Hardy, 1998.

claim: Adult Leydig cells express INSL3.
source: Adult Leydig cells express INSL3 (Insulin-like peptide 3) (Balvers et al., 1998; Mendis-Handagama et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Balvers et al., 1998 and Mendis-Handagama et al., 2007.

claim: Adult Leydig cells express SULT1E1, which protects Leydig cells and seminiferous tubules against estrogen overstimulation.
source: as well as SULT1E1 (estrogen sulfotransferase) (Sararols et al., 2021), which protects Leydig cells and seminiferous tubules against estrogen overstimulation by catalyzing the sulfoconjugation and inactivation of estrogens.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sararols et al., 2021.

claim: Estrogens and androgens can be inactivated in the testis by 17β-HSD2, which converts estradiol to estrone and testosterone to androstenedione.
source: Estrogens and androgens can also be inactivated in the testis by 17β-HSD2 (17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2), which converts estradiol to estrone and testosterone to androstenedione (Wu et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 1993.

claim: DHH is required for both proliferation and differentiation of stem Leydig cells.
source: DHH is required for both proliferation and differentiation of stem Leydig cells (Li et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2016.

claim: IGF1 stimulates the proliferation of progenitor Leydig cells and immature Leydig cells.
source: IGF1 stimulates the proliferation of progenitor Leydig cells and immature Leydig cells (Hu et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hu et al., 2010.

claim: IGF1 promotes the maturation of immature Leydig cells into adult Leydig cells.
source: and promotes the maturation of immature Leydig cells into adult Leydig cells (Wang et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2003.

claim: LH is critical to both adult Leydig cell differentiation and their precursor proliferation.
source: and LH is critical to both adult Leydig cell differentiation and their precursor proliferation (Ma et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ma et al., 2004.

claim: Testosterone is essential for many aspects of spermatogenesis, including meiotic progression, spermiogenesis, and germ cell survival.
source: Testosterone, synthesized under the control of LH, is essential for many aspects of spermatogenesis, including meiotic progression, spermiogenesis, and germ cell survival (De Gendt et al., 2004; Chang et al., 2004; Holdcraft and Braun, 2004; O'Shaughnessy et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Androgen-binding protein (ABP), produced by Sertoli cells under the regulation of FSH, increases the accumulation of androgens in the seminiferous epithelium.
source: Androgen-binding protein (ABP), produced by Sertoli cells under the regulation of FSH, increases the accumulation of androgens in the seminiferous epithelium and makes them available for binding to intracellular AR (Hagenäs et al., 1975).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hagenäs et al., 1975.

claim: Estrogens have been shown to be important for the long-term maintenance of spermatogenesis in the ArKO mouse and for the progression of normal germ cell development in the ENERKI mouse.
source: Estrogens, derived from the aromatization of androgens by CYP19A1 (aromatase) in somatic and germ cells, have been shown to be important for the long-term maintenance of spermatogenesis in the ArKO mouse (lacking aromatase) and for the progression of normal germ cell development in the ENERKI mouse (estrogen nonresponsive ERα knock-in) (Robertson et al., 1999; Sinkevicius et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Robertson et al., 1999 and Sinkevicius et al., 2009.

claim: The expression of aromatase is age-dependent, being mostly in Sertoli cells in immature rat testes and then in Leydig cells during adulthood.
source: The expression of aromatase is age-dependent, being mostly in Sertoli cells in immature rat testes and then in Leydig cells during adulthood (Rommerts et al., 1982; Papadopoulos et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rommerts et al., 1982 and Papadopoulos et al., 1986.

claim: In mouse, aromatase is present within seminiferous tubules, mainly in spermatids.
source: In mouse, aromatase is also present within seminiferous tubules, mainly in spermatids (Nitta et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nitta et al., 1993.

claim: Rhox5 encodes a transcription factor that indirectly promotes germ cell survival.
source: Rhox5, encoding a transcription factor that indirectly promotes germ cell survival (MacLean et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to MacLean et al., 2005.

claim: Rhox5 and Eppin are target genes of testosterone in Sertoli cells, with androgen response elements (ARE) in their promoters.
source: Rhox5, encoding a transcription factor that indirectly promotes germ cell survival (MacLean et al., 2005), and Eppin, encoding a serine protease inhibitor, are target genes of testosterone in Sertoli cells, with androgen response elements (ARE) in their promoters (Willems et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Willems et al., 2010.

claim: In rodents, ERα was found in Leydig cells and peritubular myoid cells.
source: In rodents, ERα was found in Leydig cells and peritubular myoid cells, ERβ was found in Sertoli cells and some germ cells (spermatogonia, spermatocytes), and GPER was detected in Leydig cells, Sertoli cells, and germ cells (spermatocytes, spermatids) (Zhou et al., 2002; Kotula-Balak et al., 2018; Lucas et al., 2010; Chimento et al., 2010; Chimento et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Faah is a direct target gene of estrogens in mature Sertoli cells.
source: Faah, encoding a hydrolase that promotes Sertoli cell survival by degrading anandamide, is a direct target gene of estrogens in mature Sertoli cells (Grimaldi et al., 2012; Rossi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Grimaldi et al., 2012 and Rossi et al., 2007.

claim: Septin12 has been identified as a potential novel target of the androgen and estrogen receptors in human testicular cells.
source: Septin12, containing 1 AR and 2 ERα binding sites in its promoter, has been identified as a potential novel target of the androgen and estrogen receptors in human testicular cells (Kuo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kuo et al., 2019.

claim: The number of Leydig cells per cm² of testicular tissue was not significantly different between D16 and 22 dpp.
source: After 16 days of culture, the number of Leydig cells per cm² of testicular tissue was not significantly different from 22 dpp, the age-matched in vivo control (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At D16, the percentage of apoptotic Leydig cells was increased compared to the in vivo control.
source: However, at this time point, the percentage of apoptotic Leydig cells was increased compared to the in vivo control while the percentage of proliferating Leydig cells was unchanged (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The percentage of proliferating Leydig cells was unchanged at D16 compared to 22 dpp.
source: However, at this time point, the percentage of apoptotic Leydig cells was increased compared to the in vivo control while the percentage of proliferating Leydig cells was unchanged (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The percentage of Leydig cells expressing AR was similar at D16 and 22 dpp.
source: In addition, the percentage of Leydig cells expressing AR was similar at D16 and 22 dpp (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: No difference was observed in the mRNA levels of Dhh, Srd5a1 and Sult1e1 between D16 and 22 dpp.
source: Whereas no difference was observed in the mRNA levels of Dhh, Srd5a1 and Sult1e1 between D16 and 22 dpp, Igf1 and Insl3 transcripts levels were respectively higher and lower in 16 day organotypic cultures than in vivo (Figure 1F–J).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1G, H, and I.

claim: Igf1 transcript levels were higher at D16 than at 22 dpp.
source: Whereas no difference was observed in the mRNA levels of Dhh, Srd5a1 and Sult1e1 between D16 and 22 dpp, Igf1 and Insl3 transcripts levels were respectively higher and lower in 16 day organotypic cultures than in vivo (Figure 1F–J).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Insl3 transcript levels were lower at D16 than at 22 dpp.
source: Whereas no difference was observed in the mRNA levels of Dhh, Srd5a1 and Sult1e1 between D16 and 22 dpp, Igf1 and Insl3 transcripts levels were respectively higher and lower in 16 day organotypic cultures than in vivo (Figure 1F–J).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Mc2r transcripts were barely detected at D16 and 22 dpp.
source: Mc2r transcripts were barely detected at D16 and 22 dpp as well as at later time points, thereby reflecting the low amount of fetal Leydig cells in prepubertal testicular tissues (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claim: After 30 days of culture, no significant difference in the number of Leydig cells per cm² of testicular tissue was observed compared to 36 dpp.
source: After 30 days of culture, no significant difference in the number of Leydig cells per cm² of testicular tissue and in the percentages of apoptotic and proliferating Leydig cells was observed compared to 36 dpp, the corresponding in vivo time point (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The percentages of apoptotic and proliferating Leydig cells were not different between D30 and 36 dpp.
source: After 30 days of culture, no significant difference in the number of Leydig cells per cm² of testicular tissue and in the percentages of apoptotic and proliferating Leydig cells was observed compared to 36 dpp, the corresponding in vivo time point (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The percentage of Leydig cells expressing AR was comparable after in vitro or in vivo maturation at D30/36 dpp.
source: Furthermore, the percentage of Leydig cells expressing AR was comparable after in vitro or in vivo maturation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The transcript levels of Dhh were similar in in vitro and in vivo matured tissues at D30/36 dpp.
source: The transcript levels of Dhh were also similar in in vitro and in vivo matured tissues at the end of the first spermatogenic wave (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: A reduction in the mRNA levels of Igf1, Srd5a1, Sult1e1, and Insl3 was found at D30 in comparison to 36 dpp in vivo controls.
source: However, a reduction in the mRNA levels of Igf1, Srd5a1, and the two adult Leydig cell markers (Sult1e1, Insl3) was found at D30 in comparison to 36 dpp in vivo controls (Figure 1F and H–J).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1F, H, I, and J.

claim: Intratesticular INSL3 was below the detection limit in in vitro matured tissues at D30.
source: Moreover, intratesticular INSL3 was below the detection limit (<10 pg/mL) in in vitro matured tissues (Figure 1K)
evidence: This is supported by RIA measurements shown in Figure 1K.

claim: A significant elevation in the concentration of INSL3 was observed in culture medium from D22 to D30 for FT tissues.
source: and a significant elevation in the concentration of INSL3 was observed in culture medium from D22 to D30 for FT tissues (Figure 1L).
evidence: This is supported by RIA measurements shown in Figure 1L.

claim: CSF had no impact on the number of Leydig cells per cm² of tissue at 6 dpp as well as after 16 or 30 days of culture.
source: CSF had no impact on the number of Leydig cells per cm² of tissue at 6 dpp as well as after 16 or 30 days of culture (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The percentage of apoptotic Leydig cells was lower in CSF than in FT tissues at 6 dpp.
source: Although the percentage of apoptotic Leydig cells was lower in CSF than in FT tissues at 6 dpp, it was similar in CSF and FT tissues at D16 and D30 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The percentage of apoptotic Leydig cells was similar in CSF and FT tissues at D16 and D30.
source: Although the percentage of apoptotic Leydig cells was lower in CSF than in FT tissues at 6 dpp, it was similar in CSF and FT tissues at D16 and D30 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No change in the percentage of Leydig cells in proliferation or expressing AR was found after CSF.
source: Furthermore, no change in the percentage of Leydig cells in proliferation or expressing AR was found after CSF (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: Dhh and Srd5a1 mRNA levels were similar in CSF and FT tissues.
source: Moreover, Dhh and Srd5a1 mRNA levels were similar in CSF and FT tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: Igf1 transcript levels were decreased in CSF tissues at D16.
source: Igf1 transcript levels were decreased in CSF tissues at D16 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Sult1e1 mRNA levels were higher in CSF tissues at D30.
source: Furthermore, Sult1e1 mRNA levels were higher in CSF tissues at D30 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I)
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Insl3 transcript levels were higher in CSF than in FT tissues at D16 and D30.
source: and Insl3 transcript levels were higher in CSF than in FT tissues at D16 and D30 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Controlled slow freezing had no impact on the mRNA levels of all the genes examined at 6 dpp.
source: Controlled slow freezing had no impact on the mRNA levels of all the genes examined at 6 dpp, i.e., before culture (Figure 2A–I).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2A-I.

claim: At D16, the mRNA levels of Star, Cyp17a1, and Hsd17b3 were decreased in FT and CSF testicular tissues compared to 22 dpp testes.
source: At D16, the mRNA levels of Star, Cyp17a1, and Hsd17b3 were decreased in FT and CSF testicular tissues compared to 22 dpp testes (Figure 2B, F and H).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2B, F, and H.

claim: Cyp11a1 transcript levels were lower in FT tissues at D16 than at 22 dpp.
source: Cyp11a1 transcript levels were also lower in FT tissues at D16 than at 22 dpp (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Lhcgr, Hsd3b1, and Hsd17b2 transcript levels remained unchanged at D16.
source: In contrast, Lhcgr, Hsd3b1, and Hsd17b2 transcript levels remained unchanged at this time point (Figure 2A, D, I).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2A, D, and I.

claim: 3β-HSD and CYP17A1 protein levels were not different between D16 and 22 dpp.
source: 3β-HSD and CYP17A1 protein levels were not different between D16 and 22 dpp (Figure 2E and G).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2E and G.

claim: The mRNA levels of Cyp11a1, Hsd3b1, Cyp17a1, and Hsd17b2 were lower at D30 in both FT and CSF tissues than in the physiological situation.
source: The mRNA levels of Cyp11a1, Hsd3b1, Cyp17a1, and Hsd17b2 were lower at D30 in both FT and CSF tissues than in the physiological situation (Figure 2C–D, F, I).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C, D, F, and I.

claim: Despite a significant decrease in Hsd3b1 mRNA levels at D30, the protein levels of 3β-HSD were not significantly different after 30 days of culture and at 36 dpp.
source: Despite a significant decrease in Hsd3b1 mRNA levels at D30, the protein levels of 3β-HSD were not significantly different after 30 days of culture and at 36 dpp (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The expression of CYP17A1 was reduced at the protein level in both FT and CSF tissues at D30 compared to 36 dpp.
source: Western blot experiments however showed that the expression of CYP17A1 was also reduced at the protein level in both FT and CSF tissues at D30 compared to 36 dpp (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: CYP17A1 was still detectable by immunofluorescence in Leydig cells in cultured tissues.
source: This steroidogenic enzyme was still detectable by immunofluorescence in Leydig cells in cultured tissues (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Lhcgr mRNA levels were found significantly reduced at D30 in FT tissues.
source: Finally, Lhcgr mRNA levels were found significantly reduced at D30 in FT tissues (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Star and Hsd17b3 mRNA levels were reduced at D30 in CSF tissues.
source: while Star and Hsd17b3 mRNA levels were reduced at D30 in CSF tissues (Figure 2B and H).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2B and H.

claim: The intratesticular concentrations of progesterone were significantly increased at D16 and D30 in both FT and CSF tissues compared to their respective in vivo controls.
source: The intratesticular concentrations of progesterone were significantly increased at D16 and D30 in both FT and CSF tissues compared to their respective in vivo controls (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The intratesticular concentrations of androstenedione were significantly decreased at D16 in both FT and CSF tissues and at D30 in FT tissues compared to in vivo controls.
source: In contrast, the intratesticular concentrations of androstenedione were significantly decreased at D16 in both FT and CSF tissues and at D30 in FT tissues compared to in vivo controls (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The intratesticular concentrations of testosterone were not different in in vitro and in vivo matured tissues at both time points.
source: The intratesticular concentrations of testosterone were however not different in in vitro and in vivo matured tissues at both time points (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The intratesticular concentrations of estradiol were significantly higher at D16 and D30 in FT and CSF tissues than in their respective in vivo controls.
source: In addition, the intratesticular concentrations of estradiol were significantly higher at D16 and D30 in FT and CSF tissues than in their respective in vivo controls (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A significant increase in the concentrations of progesterone was observed in culture medium at D26 only.
source: In the organotypic culture medium, a significant increase in the concentrations of progesterone was observed at D26 only (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A significant elevation in the concentrations of androstenedione was observed in culture medium from D16 to D30.
source: Furthermore, a significant elevation in the concentrations of androstenedione was observed from D16 to D30 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Following a decrease in testosterone levels in the culture media between D2 and D14, an augmentation was then detected between D26 and D30.
source: Regarding testosterone, following a decrease in the levels of this androgen in the culture media between D2 and D14, an augmentation was then detected between D26 and D30 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: At D30, the concentrations of both androstenedione and testosterone were higher in the culture media of FT tissues than of CSF tissues.
source: At D30, the concentrations of both androstenedione and testosterone were higher in the culture media of FT tissues than of CSF tissues (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant change in estradiol concentrations was observed in the media between D6 and D30.
source: Regarding estradiol, no significant change in its concentrations was observed in the media between D6 and D30 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The intratesticular levels of esterified cholesterol were comparable between the different experimental conditions.
source: The intratesticular levels of esterified cholesterol were comparable between the different experimental conditions (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by cholesterol assay measurements shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Total cholesterol levels were higher in FT and CSF cultured tissues at D16 and D30 compared to their corresponding in vivo time points.
source: However, total cholesterol levels were higher in FT and CSF cultured tissues at D16 and D30 compared to their corresponding in vivo time points (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by cholesterol assay measurements shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Free cholesterol levels were increased in FT and CSF cultured tissues at D30 compared to 36 dpp and in FT tissues at D16.
source: Moreover, free cholesterol levels were increased in FT and CSF cultured tissues at D30 compared to 36 dpp and in FT tissues at D16 (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by cholesterol assay measurements shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The transcript levels of Ar were higher at D16 in FT tissues than at 22 dpp.

evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Ar transcript levels were not significantly different between D30 and 36 dpp.
source: The transcript levels of Ar, encoding the androgen receptor, were higher at D16 in FT tissues than at 22 dpp but were not significantly different between D30 and 36 dpp (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: AR protein levels were comparable at D16 in FT tissues and 22 dpp.
source: Conversely, AR protein levels were comparable at D16 in FT tissues and 22 dpp but were more elevated at D30 in both FT and CSF tissues than at 36 dpp (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: AR protein levels were more elevated at D30 in both FT and CSF tissues than at 36 dpp.
source: Conversely, AR protein levels were comparable at D16 in FT tissues and 22 dpp but were more elevated at D30 in both FT and CSF tissues than at 36 dpp (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: AR was expressed in Sertoli cells, peritubular myoid cells, and Leydig cells in 16 day and 30 day cultured tissues as well as in the corresponding in vivo controls.

claim: The transcript levels of Rhox5, Eppin, and Septin12 were decreased in FT and CSF tissues cultured for 16 days compared to 22 dpp.
source: The transcript levels of two AR-regulated genes (Rhox5, Eppin) and the AR/Erα-regulated gene Septin12 were decreased in FT and CSF tissues cultured for 16 days compared to 22 dpp (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D, E, and F.

claim: At D30, Rhox5 and Septin12 mRNA levels were still lower than in vivo.
source: At D30, Rhox5 and Septin12 mRNA levels were still lower than in vivo while Eppin mRNA levels were higher than at 36 dpp (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: At D30, Eppin mRNA levels were higher than at 36 dpp.
source: At D30, Rhox5 and Septin12 mRNA levels were still lower than in vivo while Eppin mRNA levels were higher than at 36 dpp (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: A significant increase in Abp mRNA levels was found at D16 and D30 in CSF but not in FT tissues.
source: In addition, a significant increase in Abp mRNA levels was found at D16 and D30 in CSF but not in FT tissues (Figure 4G).

claim: The expression of Cyp19a1 was drastically diminished after 30 days of culture in FT and CSF tissues compared to 36 dpp.
source: Intriguingly, the expression of Cyp19a1, encoding aromatase, was drastically diminished after 30 days of culture in FT and CSF tissues compared to 36 dpp (Figure 5A).

claim: The protein levels of CYP19A1 were reduced in both FT and CSF tissues at D16 and D30.
source: The protein levels of CYP19A1 were reduced in both FT and CSF tissues at D16 and D30 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: CYP19A1 was expressed in Leydig cells at 6 dpp and in elongated spermatids and spermatozoa at 36 dpp, whereas no expression could be detected in cultured testes.
source: CYP19A1 was expressed in Leydig cells at 6 dpp and in elongated spermatids and spermatozoa at 36 dpp, whereas no expression could be detected in cultured testes (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry images shown in Figure 5C.

claim: CYP19A1 enzymatic activity was significantly decreased in CSF cultures at D30.
source: CYP19A1 enzymatic activity was also significantly decreased in CSF cultures at D30 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by aromatase activity assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The transcript levels of Esr1, Esr2, Gper1, and Faah were significantly lower at D30 than at 36 dpp.
source: In addition, the transcript levels of the three genes encoding estrogen receptors (Esr1, Esr2, Gper1) and of the estrogen target gene Faah were significantly lower at D30 than at 36 dpp (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5E, F, G, and H.

claim: Esr1 mRNA levels were decreased at D16.
source: Esr1 mRNA levels were also decreased at D16 (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: FAAH protein levels were decreased in 16 day FT and 30 day CSF organotypic cultures.
source: FAAH protein levels were decreased in 16 day FT and 30 day CSF organotypic cultures (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Upon supplementation with 1 nM hCG, intratesticular androstenedione levels were significantly increased at D30 in FT but not CSF tissues.
source: Upon supplementation with 1 nM hCG, intratesticular androstenedione levels were significantly increased at D30 in FT but not CSF tissues (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The intratesticular testosterone levels were higher at D30 in both FT and CSF tissues following hCG supplementation.
source: The intratesticular testosterone levels were higher at D30 in both FT and CSF tissues following hCG supplementation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A significant increase in androstenedione and testosterone concentrations was observed in the culture media of both FT and CSF tissues following hCG supplementation.
source: Moreover, a significant increase in androstenedione and testosterone concentrations was observed in the culture media of both FT and CSF tissues following hCG supplementation (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS measurements shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: The amounts of androgens released into the culture media were lower for CSF tissues than for FT tissues following hCG supplementation.
source: The amounts of androgens released into the culture media were, however, lower for CSF tissues than for FT tissues (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS measurements shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: The addition of 1 nM hCG had no impact on the transcript levels of Star, Hsd17b3, Hsd3b1, Ar, and Esr1 in both FT and CSF cultures.
source: The addition of 1 nM hCG had no impact on the transcript levels of Star, Hsd17b3, Hsd3b1, Ar, and Esr1 in both FT and CSF cultures (Figure 6F, I, J, L and P).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6F, I, J, L, and P.

claim: Hsd17b3 and Esr1 mRNA levels still remained lower upon hCG supplementation than in vivo.
source: Hsd17b3 and Esr1 mRNA levels still remained lower upon hCG supplementation than in vivo (Figure 6I and P).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6I and P.

claim: Lhcgr, Cyp11a1, Cyp19a1, Esr2, and Gper1 mRNA levels were increased after hCG supplementation in FT cultures.
source: Lhcgr, Cyp11a1, Cyp19a1, Esr2, and Gper1 mRNA levels were increased after hCG supplementation in FT cultures (Figure 6E, G–H, K, Q and R).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6E, G, H, K, Q, and R.

claim: Cyp11a1 and Cyp19a1 mRNA levels were still lower after hCG supplementation than in vivo.
source: Whereas Cyp11a1 and Cyp19a1 mRNA levels were still lower after hCG supplementation than in vivo (Figure 6G and K)
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6G and K.

claim: Esr2 and Gper1 transcripts were restored to their physiological levels after hCG supplementation.

claim: mRNA levels of Rhox5, Eppin, Septin12, and Igf1 were decreased after hCG supplementation in FT cultures.

claim: The mean proportions of seminiferous tubules containing round and elongated spermatids were lower in tissues cultured with than without hCG.
source: Finally, the mean proportions of seminiferous tubules containing round and elongated spermatids were lower in tissues cultured with than without hCG (Figure 6T).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis data shown in Figure 6T.

claim: The number of Sertoli cells inside seminiferous tubules was unchanged following hCG supplementation, but was higher than in in vivo controls.
source: The number of Sertoli cells inside seminiferous tubules was unchanged following hCG supplementation, but was higher than in in vivo controls (Figure 6U).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6U.

claim: The deficient Leydig cell maturation observed at D30 could be related to the decreased levels of Igf1.
source: The deficient Leydig cell maturation observed at D30 could be related to the decreased levels of Igf1, which encodes insulin-like growth factor 1 known to promote the maturation of immature Leydig cells into adult Leydig cells (Wang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed decrease in Igf1 and known function of IGF1.

claim: The accumulation of estradiol in in vitro cultured tissues could be deleterious for sperm production.
source: Here, we report for the first time an accumulation of estradiol in in vitro cultured tissues, which could be deleterious for sperm production.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed estradiol accumulation.

claim: The cumulative excess of progesterone and estradiol in cultured testicular tissues may slow the progression of in vitro spermatogenesis and lead to a poor sperm yield.
source: The cumulative excess of progesterone and estradiol in cultured testicular tissues may, therefore, slow the progression of in vitro spermatogenesis and lead to a poor sperm yield.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed steroid imbalances and known effects of these hormones.

claim: The increased AR protein levels at D30 could be the result of the higher number of Sertoli cells within seminiferous tubules.
source: The increased AR protein levels at D30 could thus be the result of the higher number of Sertoli cells within seminiferous tubules.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in AR protein and Sertoli cell number.

claim: AR signaling may be dysfunctional in Leydig cells in vitro.
source: This could suggest that AR signaling is dysfunctional in Leydig cells in vitro.
evidence: This is an inference based on similarities with LCARKO mice.

claim: AR signaling may be impaired in Sertoli cells in organotypic cultures.
source: The downregulation of Rhox5 expression (Figure 7), which confirms our previous findings (Rondanino et al., 2017), further suggests that AR signaling may also be impaired in Sertoli cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the downregulation of Rhox5, an AR target gene.

claim: The transcription of Cyp19a1, Esr1, and Esr2 may be negatively controlled by elevated estradiol levels in tissue cultures.
source: Since the expression of Cyp19a1, Esr1, and Esr2 (encoding aromatase, ERα, and ERβ, respectively) can be downregulated by estradiol in the rat testis (Zanatta et al., 2021; Genissel et al., 2001), we hypothesize that the transcription of these genes may be negatively controlled by elevated estradiol levels in our tissue cultures.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on known regulatory mechanisms and observed estradiol levels.

claim: The decreased Faah transcript levels in organotypic cultures could be the consequence of the downregulated ERβ expression and/or of the immaturity of Sertoli cells.
source: Thus, the decreased Faah transcript levels in organotypic cultures could be the consequence of the downregulated ERβ expression and/or of the immaturity of Sertoli cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on known regulation of Faah and observed ERβ levels.

claim: The transcription of Insl3 could be inhibited by the excess of estradiol in tissue cultures.
source: The transcription of Insl3, which is repressed by estradiol in an MA-10 Leydig cell line model (Laguë and Tremblay, 2009), could also be inhibited by the excess of estradiol in our tissue cultures.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on known regulation of Insl3 and observed estradiol levels.

claim: Estrogen excess in organotypic cultures could be explained by low Sult1e1 expression.
source: In organotypic cultures, estrogen excess could be explained by low Sult1e1 expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the function of SULT1E1 and observed expression levels.

claim: Reduced transcript levels of Hsd17b2 may explain why estradiol levels remain elevated in cultures while testosterone levels are similar to controls and androstenedione levels are low.
source: In addition, reduced transcript levels of Hsd17b2, encoding an enzyme that converts estradiol to estrone and testosterone to androstenedione, may also explain why estradiol levels remain elevated in cultures while testosterone levels are similar to controls and androstenedione levels are low.
evidence: This is an inference based on the function of HSD17B2 and observed steroid levels.
